## Invasive Species: The Battle for Ecological Balance

The visitor who walks the trails of the Charca de Suárez in spring can hardly imagine that beneath the apparent serenity of the landscape a silent battle is being waged. The sheets of water reflecting the reeds and moorhens hide a persistent threat that demands constant human intervention. The wetland's technicians know the three main enemies well: the common reed, the water hyacinth, and the Florida turtle.

The common reed, *Arundo donax* in its scientific designation, represents the most visible challenge for any attentive walker. This grass of Asian origin colonizes the shores with an aggressiveness that suffocates native vegetation, especially the common reed and cattail that serve as refuge for marsh birds. Its uncontrolled growth reduces the usable surface of the lagoons and modifies the light and humidity conditions needed by species native to the Mediterranean coast. Manual extraction and selective mowing work have become a seasonal routine that the management team executes with surgical precision.

The water hyacinth, *Eichhornia crassipes*, poses a different but equally severe problem. This floating plant native to the Amazon basin reproduces at a rate that surprises even experienced biologists. A single clump can double its surface area in less than two weeks when temperatures are favorable, forming dense mats that prevent sunlight from reaching the bottom of the ponds. The direct consequence is eutrophication of the water bodies, a process that depletes dissolved oxygen and causes the death of fish, amphibians, and aquatic invertebrates. Workers remove the specimens manually before massive flowering makes the plague uncontrollable.

The third threat has a shell and a voracious appetite. The Florida turtle, *Trachemys scripta*, arrived in Spanish wetlands through the pet trade and irresponsible releases by private individuals. At the Charca de Suárez it competes with the native Spanish terrapin for basking sites and food, in addition to directly preying on waterbird nests and tadpoles. Its capture requires selective trapping with floating fyke nets and basking platforms, a method that allows specimens to be removed without harming the native species sharing the habitat.

The figures from the last fiscal year give a measure of the effort invested. During 2023, more than five tons of common reed were removed from the shores and the connection channels between lagoons. The extracted volume equals the weight of three compact cars and requires a dedicated logistics system for transport and management of plant debris. In parallel, chelonian trapping allowed the capture of two hundred Florida turtle specimens, a figure that evidences the magnitude of the problem inherited from decades of uncontrolled releases.

Coordination of these tasks falls to a small but specialized team that combines knowledge of botany, herpetology, and wetland management. The action calendar is designed each year based on the biological cycles of invasive species and the protected birds that nest in the enclave. Reed mowing is concentrated in the autumn and winter months to avoid interfering with the reproduction of marsh birds, while water hyacinth removal is intensified between June and September, when heat accelerates its expansion.

Complete eradication of these species is technically impossible in the short term, but the managers' goal is to keep their populations below the threshold of ecological damage. Each hectare of reedbed recovered means available habitat for the purple heron and the common moorhen. Each exotic turtle removed reduces pressure on the nests of the little grebe and on native amphibian populations. The battle for ecological balance is measured in small victories that rarely reach the general public.

The Interpretation Center incorporates this issue into its educational discourse with specific panels and teaching materials. Schoolchildren visiting the wetland learn to distinguish the invasive reed from the native common reed and understand why they should not release exotic pets into the natural environment. Environmental education thus becomes a preventive tool that complements fieldwork and reduces the arrival of new invasive specimens.

The experience accumulated at the Charca de Suárez has sparked interest among other Andalusian wetland managers. The exotic turtle trapping protocol and the selective reedbed mowing system have been shared with technicians from Doñana and the Paraje Natural de la Desembocadura del Guadalhorce. Collaboration between teams allows refining methodologies and adapting intervention calendars to the particularities of each enclave.

The future of this battle depends on budgetary consistency and continuous vigilance. A single year of neglect would allow the reed to regain lost ground and the water hyacinth to cover the water bodies again within weeks. The managers know this and therefore insist that wetland conservation admits no truces. The Charca de Suárez maintains its vital pulse thanks to human intervention that, paradoxically, remains invisible to most of those who enjoy its beauty.
